vsm1.8:42.1:
Now comes the description of the development of mindfulness occupied with the body as a meditation subject,
which is never promulgated except after an Enlightened One’s arising, and is outside the province of any sectarians.
It has been commended by the Blessed One in various ways in different suttas thus:
vsm1.8:42.2:
“Bhikkhus, when one thing is developed and repeatedly practiced, it leads to a supreme
sense of urgency, to supreme benefit, to supreme surcease of bondage, to supreme mindfulness and full
awareness, to acquisition of knowledge and vision, to a happy life here and now, to realization of the fruit of clear
vision and deliverance. What is that one thing? It is mindfulness occupied with the body” (A I 43).
vsm1.8:42.3:
And thus: “Bhikkhus, they savour the deathless who savour mindfulness occupied with the body; they do not savour
the deathless who do not savour mindfulness occupied with the body. They have savoured the deathless who have savoured
mindfulness occupied with the body; they have not savoured … They have neglected … they have not neglected … They
have missed … they have found the deathless who have found mindfulness occupied with the body” (A I 45).
vsm1.8:42.4:
And it has been described in fourteen sections in the passage beginning, “And how developed, bhikkhus, how repeatedly practiced
is mindfulness occupied with the body of great fruit, of great benefit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest …” (M III 89),
vsm1.8:42.5:
that is to say, the sections on breathing, on postures, on the four kinds of full awareness, on attention
directed to repulsiveness, on attention directed to elements, and on the nine charnel-ground contemplations.
vsm1.8:43.1:
Herein, the three, that is to say, the sections on postures, on the four kinds of full awareness (see M-a I
253f.), and on attention directed to elements, as they are stated in that sutta, deal with insight.
vsm1.8:43.2:
Then the nine sections on the charnel-ground contemplations, as stated there,
deal with that particular phase of insight knowledge called contemplation of danger.
vsm1.8:43.3:
And any development of concentration in the bloated, etc., that might be implied there
has already been explained in the Description of Foulness (Ch. VI).
vsm1.8:43.4:
So there are only the two, that is, the sections on breathing and on directing
attention to repulsiveness, that, as stated there, deal with concentration.
vsm1.8:43.5: Of these two, the section on breathing is a separate meditation subject, namely, mindfulness of breathing.
vsm1.8:44.1:
What is intended here as mindfulness occupied with the body is the thirty-two aspects. This meditation subject is taught
as the direction of attention to repulsiveness thus: “Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this body, up from the soles of the feet
and down from the top of the hair and contained in the skin, as full of many kinds of filth thus: In this body there are head hairs,
body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidney, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels,
entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine”
(M III 90), the brain being included in the bone marrow in this version with a total of only thirty-one aspects.
vsm1.8:45.1: Here is the description of the development introduced by a commentary on the text.
vsm1.8:45.2: This body: this filthy body constructed out of the four primary elements.
vsm1.8:45.3: Up from the soles of the feet: from the soles of the feet upwards.
vsm1.8:45.4: Down from the top of the hair: from the highest part of the hair downwards.
vsm1.8:45.5: Contained in the skin: terminated all round by the skin.
vsm1.8:45.6:
Reviews … as full of many kinds of filth: he sees that this body
is packed with the filth of various kinds beginning with head hairs.
vsm1.8:45.7: How? “In this body there are head hairs … urine.”
vsm1.8:46.1: Herein, there are means, there are found.
vsm1.8:46.2:
In this: in this, which is expressed thus: “Up from the soles of the feet and down from the top
of the hair and contained in the skin, as full of many kinds of filth.”
vsm1.8:46.3:
Body: the carcass; for it is the carcass that is called “body” (kāya) because it is a conglomeration of filth, because such vile
(kucchita) things as the head hairs, etc., and the hundred diseases beginning with eye disease, have it as their origin (āya).
vsm1.8:46.4: Head hairs, body hairs: these things beginning with head hairs are the thirty-two aspects.
vsm1.8:46.5: The construction here should be understood in this way: In this body there are head hairs, in this body there are body hairs.
vsm1.8:47.2:
on the contrary he finds nothing but the various very malodorous, offensive, drab-looking
sorts of filth consisting of the head hairs, body hairs, and the rest.
vsm1.8:47.3: Hence it is said: “In this body there are head hairs, body hairs … urine.”
vsm1.8:47.4: This is the commentary on the word-construction here.
vsm1.8:48.1:
Now, a clansman who, as a beginner, wants to develop this meditation subject should go to a good
friend of the kind already described (III.61–73) and learn it.
vsm1.8:48.2: And the teacher who expounds it to him should tell him the sevenfold skill in learning and the tenfold skill in giving attention.
vsm1.8:48.3:
Herein, the sevenfold skill in learning should be told thus: (1) as verbal recitation, (2) as mental recitation,
(3) as to colour, (4) as to shape, (5) as to direction, (6) as to location, (7) as to delimitation.
vsm1.8:49.1:
1. This meditation subject consists in giving attention to repulsiveness. Even if one is master of the Tipiṭaka,
the verbal recitation should still be done at the time of first giving it attention.
vsm1.8:49.2:
For the meditation subject only becomes evident to some through recitation, as it did to the two elders
who learned the meditation subject from the Elder Mahā Deva of the Hill Country (Malaya).
vsm1.8:49.3:
On being asked for the meditation subject, it seems, the elder gave the text of the thirty-two
aspects, saying, “Do only this recitation for four months.”
vsm1.8:49.4:
Although they were familiar respectively with two and three Piṭakas, it was only at the end of four
months of recitation of the meditation subject that they became stream-enterers, with right apprehension of the text.
vsm1.8:49.5: So the teacher who expounds the meditation subject should tell the pupil to do the recitation verbally first.
vsm1.8:50.1: Now, when he does the recitation, he should divide it up into the “skin pentad,” etc., and do it forwards and backwards.
vsm1.8:50.2:
After saying “Head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin,” he should repeat it backwards,
“Skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.”
vsm1.8:51.1:
Next to that, with the “kidney pentad,” after saying “Flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidney,” he should repeat
it backwards, “Kidney, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.”
vsm1.8:52.1:
Next, with the “lungs pentad,” after saying “Heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs,” he should repeat it backwards, “Lungs,
spleen, midriff, liver, heart; kidney, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.”
vsm1.8:56.1: The recitation should be done verbally in this way a hundred times, a thousand times, even a hundred thousand times.
vsm1.8:56.2:
For it is through verbal recitation that the meditation subject becomes familiar, and the mind
being thus prevented from running here and there,
vsm1.8:56.3: the parts become evident and seem like the fingers of a pair of clasped hands, like a row of fence posts.
vsm1.8:57.1: 2. The mental recitation should be done just as it is done verbally.
vsm1.8:57.2: For the verbal recitation is a condition for the mental recitation,
vsm1.8:57.3: and the mental recitation is a condition for the penetration of the characteristic of foulness.
vsm1.8:58.1: 3. As to colour: the colour of the head hairs, etc., should be defined.
vsm1.8:58.2: 4. As to shape: their shape should be defined too.
vsm1.8:58.3:
5. As to direction: in this body, upwards from the navel is the upward direction, and downwards from it
is the downward direction. So the direction should be defined thus: “This part is in this direction.”
vsm1.8:58.4: 6. As to location: the location of this or that part should be defined thus: “This part is established in this location.”
vsm1.8:59.1: 7. As to delimitation: there are two kinds of delimitation, that is, delimitation of the similar and delimitation of the dissimilar.
vsm1.8:59.2: Herein, delimitation of the similar should be understood in this way: “This part is delimited above and below and around by this.”
vsm1.8:59.3:
Delimitation of the dissimilar should be understood as non-intermixed-ness in this way:
“Head hairs are not body hairs, and body hairs are not head hairs.”
vsm1.8:60.1:
When the teacher tells the skill in learning in seven ways thus, he should do so knowing that in certain suttas this meditation
subject is expounded from the point of view of repulsiveness and in certain suttas from the point of view of elements.
vsm1.8:60.2: For in the Mahā Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (DN 22) it is expounded only as repulsiveness.
vsm1.8:60.3:
In the Mahā Hatthipadopama Sutta (MN 28), in the Mahā Rāhulovāda Sutta (MN 62), and the Dhātuvibhaṅga
(MN 140, also Vibh 82), it is expounded as elements.
vsm1.8:60.4:
In the Kāyagatāsati Sutta (MN 119), however, four jhānas are expounded with reference to one to whom
it has appeared as a colour kasiṇa (see III.107).
vsm1.8:60.5: Herein, it is an insight meditation subject that is expounded as elements
vsm1.8:60.6: and a serenity meditation subject that is expounded as repulsiveness.
vsm1.8:60.7: Consequently it is only the serenity meditation subject that is relevant here.
vsm1.8:61.1:
Having thus told the sevenfold skill in learning, he should tell the tenfold skill in giving attention as follows:
(1) as to following the order, (2) not too quickly, (3) not too slowly (4) as to warding off distraction,
(5) as to surmounting the concept, (6) as to successive leaving, (7) as to absorption, (8)–(10) as to the three suttantas.
vsm1.8:62.1:
1. Herein, as to following the order: from the time of beginning the recitation attention
should be given following the serial order without skipping.
vsm1.8:62.2:
For just as when someone who has no skill climbs a thirty-two-rung ladder using every other step, his body gets exhausted and he
falls without completing the climb, so too, one who gives it attention skipping parts becomes exhausted in his mind and does
not complete the development since he fails to get the satisfaction that ought to be got with successful development.
vsm1.8:63.1: 2. Also when he gives attention to it following the serial order, he should do so not too quickly.
vsm1.8:63.2:
For just as when a man sets out on a three-league journey, even if he has already done the journey out and back
a hundred times rapidly without taking note of turnings to be taken and avoided, though he may finish his journey,
he still has to ask how to get there, so too, when the meditator gives his attention to the meditation
subject too quickly, though he may reach the end of the meditation subject, it still does not become
clear or bring about any distinction. So he should not give his attention to it too quickly.
vsm1.8:64.1: 3. And as “not too quickly,” so also not too slowly.
vsm1.8:64.2:
For just as when a man wants to do a three-league journey in one day, if he loiters on the way among trees, rocks, pools,
etc., he does not finish the journey in a day and needs two or three to complete it, so too, if the meditator gives
his attention to the meditation subject too slowly, he does not get to the end and it does not become a condition for distinction.
vsm1.8:65.1:
4. As to warding off distraction: he must ward off temptation to drop the meditation
subject and to let his mind get distracted among the variety of external objects.
vsm1.8:65.2:
For if not, just as when a man has entered on a one-foot-wide cliff path, if he looks about here and there without
watching his step, he may miss his footing and fall down the cliff, which is perhaps as high as a hundred men,
so too, when there is outward distraction, the meditation subject gets neglected and deteriorates.
vsm1.8:65.3: So he should give his attention to it warding off distraction.
vsm1.8:66.1:
5. As to surmounting the concept: this name- concept beginning with “head hairs, body hairs”
must be surmounted and consciousness established on the aspect “repulsive.”
vsm1.8:66.2:
For just as when men find a water hole in a forest in a time of drought, they hang up some kind of signal
there such as a palm leaf, and people come to bathe and drink guided by the signal,
vsm1.8:66.3:
but when the way has become plain with their continual traffic, there is no further
need of the signal and they go to bathe and drink there whenever they want,
vsm1.8:66.4:
so too, when repulsiveness becomes evident to him as he is giving his attention to the meditation subject
through the means of the name- concept “head hairs, body hairs,” he must surmount the concept “head hairs,
body hairs” and establish consciousness on only the actual repulsiveness.
vsm1.8:67.1: 6. As to successive leaving: in giving his attention he should eventually leave out any parts that do not appear to him.
vsm1.8:67.2:
For when a beginner gives his attention to head hairs, his attention then carries on till
it arrives at the last part, that is, urine and stops there;
vsm1.8:67.3:
and when he gives his attention to urine, his attention then carries on till it arrives
back at the first part, that is, head hairs, and stops there.
vsm1.8:67.4: As he persists in giving his attention thus, some parts appear to him and others do not.
vsm1.8:67.5: Then he should work on those that have appeared till one out of any two appears the clearer.
vsm1.8:67.6: He should arouse absorption by again and again giving attention to the one that has appeared thus.
